name: Thanthondriappar Temple, Akkur
deity: Shiva as Thanthondriappar (the self-manifested lord), with the goddess Valnedunkanni
tradition: Shaiva — a Paadal Petra Sthalam, a Maada Kovil
period: Tevaram era; traditionally a Kochengat Chola Maada Kovil
summary: Akkur, east of Mayiladuthurai, honours Shiva as Thanthondriappar — the self-manifested lord — whose lingam is said to have risen of its own accord as a temple tank was being dug. A Paadal Petra Sthalam sung by Sambandar and Appar, it is known in the hymns as Thon-Thondri Maadam and was built as a raised Maada Kovil, by tradition one of those of the Chola king Kochengat Chola. The village is also the birthplace of Sirappuli Nayanar, one of the sixty-three Shaiva saints.

sections.history: Akkur, east of Mayiladuthurai on the road toward Tharangambadi, is an ancient Shaiva village hymned in the seventh-century Tevaram by Sambandar and Appar and counted among the Paadal Petra Sthalams, where it is named Thon-Thondri Maadam. The temple was built as a Maada Kovil — a raised temple of the type traditionally ascribed to the early Chola king Kochengat Chola — and the village holds the added honour of being the birthplace of Sirappuli Nayanar, one of the sixty-three Shaiva saints.
sections.architecture: As a Maada Kovil the temple sits on an elevated base, reached by steps, in the manner of the Kochengat Chola foundations built high so that an elephant could not enter the sanctum. The sanctum enshrines the self-manifested lingam of Thanthondriappar, and the goddess Valnedunkanni has her own shrine. The temple's Murugan, praised by the saint-poet Arunagirinathar in his Tiruppugazh, adds to the devotional draw of the raised village shrine.
sections.legends: The name Thanthondriappar — 'the lord who appeared of himself' — comes from the tradition that the lingam rose on its own as a tank was being dug before the temple. A second story tells of a Chola king, in some tellings Kochengat Chola, afflicted with a disease no physician could cure; Shiva came to him in a dream and bade him feed a thousand people for forty-eight days, and on fulfilling this the king was healed and raised the Maada Kovil here. The village's honour as the birthplace of Sirappuli Nayanar binds it further into the story of the Shaiva saints.
sections.festivals: The temple keeps the Shaiva festival calendar — Maha Shivaratri, Pradosham, the Margazhi season and the annual Brahmotsavam — and the day of Sirappuli Nayanar is observed with special honour as the saint's native place. The raised sanctum gives the festival processions their own character among the delta villages.
sections.experience: Climbing to the elevated sanctum of a Maada Kovil is part of the pilgrimage at Akkur, and the darshan of the self-manifested Thanthondriappar carries the sense of a lord who came forth of his own will. The village's link to Sirappuli Nayanar and to the healing of a king gives this quiet shrine a depth beyond its modest size.

visit.timings: Typically open from early morning to midday and again from late afternoon into the evening; confirm timings locally, especially on festival days.
visit.dressCode: Modest traditional attire is expected, with shoulders and knees covered; footwear is left at the entrance.
visit.photography: Photography is generally allowed in the outer corridors but not inside the sanctum; ask temple staff before photographing rituals.
visit.gettingThere: Akkur (Tiru-Aakkur) is about 16 km east of Mayiladuthurai on the Mayiladuthurai–Tharangambadi road, Mayiladuthurai district; the nearest rail head is Mayiladuthurai, with local buses and taxis to the village.
